To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
category competition can sharpen boundaries between categories.
Category competition, a cognitively general phenomenon, can act to sharpen category boundaries, which may have contributed to language evolution.

category competition as a driver for contrast is a general cognitive mechanism, that is, it applies to any behavior that is learned by imitation, and that the mechanism is likely to have contributed to the evolution of human language.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the human language faculty, and in particular with the origin of its combinatorial nature.
the evolution of human language, and in particular with the evolution of the ability to maintain large numbers of distinct signal/meanings categories.
the evolution of the human capacity for complex language, and the evolution of language itself.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evolution of language is the result of the interplay of several mechanisms, including those related to social learning, the ability to categorize, and to contrast.
the evolution of the language capacity was driven by a combination of the evolution of the brain and the evolution of the culture.
the category competition is the driving force behind the evolution of category contrasts.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
category contrast, as well as category competition, are important for the evolution of categories, and category competition can promote category contrast.
the perception–production feedback can be a powerful mechanism for the evolution of language, and the evolution of language is a powerful mechanism for evolution of the brain.
the perception-production feedback loop is a driver of category evolution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of categories is not a passive process, but rather can be actively driven by the way in which they are perceived.
the ability of the mind to maintain a large set of distinct mental categories may have been a prerequisite for the evolution of language.
the ability to maintain distinct categories is not just a matter of perceptual acuity, but also of behavioral plasticity and learning.
